title: Stage 1: The master key
summary: Turn a master password into a key with PBKDF2, prove a password is right without storing it, and lock and unlock the vault.

steps.title: What you are building
body: Over five stages you will build a **password vault**: a console program that reads commands from standard input, one per line, keeps everything in memory, and prints one result per command. The tests feed it a script of commands and check every line it prints.

By stage 5 it has envelope encryption, sharing between users, key rotation, a tamper-evident audit log and an encrypted export. Every piece is a pattern real systems use: 1Password, Bitwarden, cloud KMS and database encryption are all built from these parts.
**Stage 1** is the root of it all: the **master key**. The vault never stores the password or the key. It stores a *key-check value* that proves a password is right.

steps.prompt: Why does the vault store a key-check value instead of the master key or a plain SHA-256 of the password?
options: Storing the key would let anyone who reads the file decrypt everything, and a fast hash of a password can be brute-forced quickly; a key-check from a slow KDF proves the password without revealing the key
Because SHA-256 output is too long to store
Because the key-check can be decrypted back into the password if the user forgets it
Because HMAC is faster than SHA-256
steps.explain: The stored value must be useless to a thief: it reveals nothing about the key (HMAC is one-way) and checking each password guess costs a full PBKDF2 run. Password storage itself is covered in depth by the *Authentication & JWT* topic.

steps.title: The spec
body: The starter has the command loop and a `Vault` class. Implement:
| `lock` | `locked`, and the key is wiped from memory |
The master key is **PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256** of the password's UTF-8 bytes with the salt `"dojo-vault-salt1"` (UTF-8), **1,000** iterations, 32 bytes:

The **key-check** is `HMACSHA256(masterKey, UTF8("key-check"))`. Store all 32 bytes; print only the first 4 as lowercase hex (`Convert.ToHexStringLower(value, 0, 4)`). `unlock` derives a candidate key and compares key-checks with `CryptographicOperations.FixedTimeEquals`.
- `init` when a vault exists: `error: vault already exists`; with no password: `error: missing argument`; under 8 characters: `error: password too short`
- anything else: `error: unknown command` (already in the starter)
> **Tip:** 1,000 iterations and a fixed salt keep the tests fast and the output repeatable. A real vault uses 600,000+ iterations (or Argon2) and a **random** salt saved next to the vault file.

steps.prompt: PBKDF2 is deterministic: the same password, salt and iteration count always give the same key. What does this print?
steps.explain: Determinism is what lets `unlock` re-derive the same key. The salt changes everything, which is why a real vault uses a random one: two users with the same password get unrelated keys, and precomputed tables are useless.

steps.prompt: Arrange the body of `Unlock` (after the `no vault` check).
steps.explain: Derive, check in constant time, and only then keep the key. A key that failed the check is never stored.

steps.title: Derive, check, lock
prompt: Implement stage 1 as specified on the cards above (`init`, `unlock`, `lock`, `status`). Keep the command loop: it prints whatever `Run` returns.
The tests run whole command scripts. For example, this input:
starter: // Tests only: a real vault uses 600,000+ iterations and a random salt stored next to the vault.
byte[]? keyCheck;    // stored with the vault: proves a password is right without storing the key
byte[]? masterKey;   // only in memory, only while unlocked
string Arg(int i) => i < parts.Length ? parts[i] : "";
// Derive the master key with PBKDF2, store its key-check, stay unlocked.
// Derive a candidate key and compare key-checks in constant time.
solution: // Tests only: a real vault uses 600,000+ iterations and a random salt stored next to the vault.
byte[]? keyCheck;    // stored with the vault: proves a password is right without storing the key
byte[]? masterKey;   // only in memory, only while unlocked
string Arg(int i) => i < parts.Length ? parts[i] : "";
"status" => keyCheck is null ? "no vault" : masterKey is null ? "locked" : "unlocked",
static byte[] KeyCheck(byte[] key) => HMACSHA256.HashData(key, Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("key-check"));
if (keyCheck is not null) return "error: vault already exists";
if (keyCheck is null) return "error: no vault";
if (keyCheck is null) return "error: no vault";

tests.name: lock, a wrong password, then the right one
tests.stdin:
init correct-horse
lock
status
unlock wrong-horse
status
unlock correct-horse
status

tests.name: errors before and after init
tests.stdin:
status
unlock whatever
lock
init short
init
init correct-horse
init another-password
fly

tests.name: a different password gives a different key-check
tests.stdin:
init Tr0ub4dor&3
lock
unlock correct-horse
unlock Tr0ub4dor&3

hints: Write two helpers: `static byte[] DeriveKey(string password)` and `static byte[] KeyCheck(byte[] key) => HMACSHA256.HashData(key, Encoding.UTF8.GetBytes("key-check"))`.
`status` is `keyCheck is null ? "no vault" : masterKey is null ? "locked" : "unlocked"`.
In `Lock`, call `CryptographicOperations.ZeroMemory(masterKey)` before setting it to null.
